author: Dionysius of Corinth
addressee: Various churches and individuals: Rome, Lacedaemon, Athens, Nicomedia, Gortyna and Crete, Amastris and Pontus, Cnossus, and a woman named Chrysophora
occasion: Dionysius wrote pastoral letters to churches and individuals across the Greek world, addressing local needs, encouraging orthodoxy, and responding to requests from fellow believers. Some of his letters were later tampered with by heretics, prompting him to note the corruption.
argument: Dionysius praises the Roman church for its inherited custom of sending aid to needy brethren and churches, especially under Bishop Soter. He recalls reading the Romans' letter on the Lord's day and says they will keep reading it for admonition, just as they do with the former letter written through Clement. He praises the Romans and Corinthians for having blended together the planting made by Peter and Paul, who taught together in Italy and were martyred at the same time. He warns that his own letters have been corrupted by agents of the devil, who added and removed material. The fragments also catalogue his letters to various churches, showing his wide pastoral concern for orthodoxy, peace, and moral discipline.

outline.move: Dionysius praises the Romans for their ancestral custom of sending aid to the saints and commends Bishop Soter for increasing it.
He recalls reading the Romans' letter on the Lord's day and says they will keep reading it for admonition, as they do with the former letter written through Clement.
He praises the Romans and Corinthians for having blended together the planting made by Peter and Paul, who taught together in Italy and were martyred at the same time.
He complains that his own letters have been tampered with by apostles of the devil, who added and removed material.
Eusebius catalogues Dionysius's letters to Lacedaemon, Athens, Nicomedia, Gortyna, Amastris, Cnossus, and Chrysophora, summarizing their contents.

cast.name: Soter
cast.who: Bishop of Rome praised by Dionysius for his generosity and pastoral care.

cast.name: Clement
cast.who: Author of an earlier letter to the Corinthians, read publicly in Corinth.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: Apostle who, with Paul, planted the church in Corinth and taught in Italy.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: Apostle who, with Peter, planted the church in Corinth and taught in Italy.

cast.name: Publius
cast.who: Leader of the Athenian church who was martyred during the persecutions. The source does not explicitly call him bishop.

cast.name: Quadratus
cast.who: Bishop of Athens after the martyred Publius, credited with gathering the church and reviving its faith.

cast.name: Dionysius the Areopagite
cast.who: Converted by Paul and first bishop of the church in Athens.

cast.name: Philip
cast.who: Bishop of Gortyna in Crete, commended by Dionysius.

cast.name: Bacchylides
cast.who: One of two men who urged Dionysius to write to the church at Amastris.

cast.name: Elpistus
cast.who: One of two men who urged Dionysius to write to the church at Amastris.

cast.name: Palmas
cast.who: Bishop of Amastris, mentioned by Dionysius.

cast.name: Pinytus
cast.who: Bishop of Cnossus, urged by Dionysius not to impose a heavy burden of chastity on the brethren.

cast.name: Chrysophora
cast.who: A faithful sister to whom Dionysius wrote a letter of spiritual nourishment.

scripture: Dionysius refers to 'the Lord's day' (ἡ Κυριακὴ ἁγία ἡμέρα) for the day of worship. He mentions 'the divine writings' (γραφαὶ θεῖαι) and 'the Lord's writings' (αἱ Κυριακαὶ γραφαί), but no specific Old Testament or New Testament books are cited by name in the fragments. Eusebius refers to 'the Acts' (αἱ πράξεις) for the conversion of Dionysius the Areopagite by Paul.
uncertain: The exact date of Dionysius's episcopate; c. 170 is approximate based on Eusebius's chronology.
The precise wording of Dionysius's original letters, since the fragments are preserved only in Eusebius's quotations and summaries.
The identity of Chrysophora beyond her being a faithful sister.
Whether the letter to Nicomedia is genuinely by Dionysius, since Eusebius says it is 'reported' (φέρεται).
The exact nature and extent of the tampering with Dionysius's letters mentioned in section 4.
Whether the Quadratus mentioned as bishop of Athens is the famous Quadratus or a later bishop of the same name.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He recalls reading the Romans' letter on the Lord's day and says they will keep reading it for admonition, just as they do with the former letter written through Clement.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὴν σήμερον οὖν Κυριακὴν ἁγίαν ἡμέραν διηγάγομεν, ἐν ᾗ ἀνέγνωμεν ὑμῶν τὴν ἐπιστολήν· ἣν ἕξομεν ἀεί ποτε ἀναγινώσκοντες νουθετεῖσθαι, ὡς καὶ τὴν προτέραν ἡμῖν διὰ Κλήμεντος γραφεῖσαν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: He recalls that on the Lord's day they read the Romans' letter, and says they will always have it to read for admonition, as they do with the former letter written to us through Clement.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He praises the Romans and Corinthians for having blended together the planting made by Peter and Paul, who taught together in Italy and were martyred at the same time.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὴν ἀπὸ Πέτρου καὶ Παύλου φυτείαν γενηθεῖσαν Ῥωμαίων τε καὶ Κορινθίων συνεκεράσατε
_unresolved_facts.fix: He praises the Romans and Corinthians for having blended together the planting made by Peter and Paul (which came to be of Romans and Corinthians); for both planted in Corinth and taught alike, and likewise taught together in Italy and were martyred at the same time.

_unresolved_facts.fix: The source calls him 'the one presiding over them' (τὸν προεστῶτα αὐτῶν), which is an ecclesiastical leadership term, though 'bishop' is not explicitly used.
